title: Two rounds of review without losing the reviewer's place
summary: Push, get comments, respond, get more comments, respond again, then land it clean. The whole argument about force-pushing during review, settled by looking at what each option does to the diff.
mental_model: During review, extra commits are kind to the reviewer — they can see just what changed since last time. Before merging, a clean series is kind to everyone afterwards. Do the first during, the second at the end.

write.content:
def total(items):
    return sum(i['price'] for i in items)

steps.title: Open the review
steps.why: Two commits, each doing one thing, pushed to a branch. That push is the pull request; everything after it is conversation.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Apply discounts to order totals"

verify.label: two commits are up for review

steps.title: The reviewer reads it in their own clone
steps.why: Fetching the branch and reading the three-dot diff is what the web interface shows, minus the comment boxes. Reviewing commit by commit — `git log -p` — is usually faster than reading one combined diff.
steps.expect: The branch's two commits and the resulting file.

steps.title: Round one: respond with a new commit
steps.why: The reviewer wants validation. Adding a commit — rather than amending — means their next look is a two-line diff instead of the whole branch again. This is the single most useful courtesy in code review.
steps.expect: Three commits, pushed as an ordinary fast-forward — no force needed.

verify.label: the response is a visible third commit

steps.title: The reviewer sees exactly what changed
steps.why: Because nothing was rewritten, the reviewer can diff their last-seen tip against the new one. Two lines to re-review instead of eighty — and this is impossible if you amended.
commands: sh -c 'old=$(git rev-parse origin/feature/discounts); git fetch -q origin; git diff --stat $old origin/feature/discounts; git log --oneline $old..origin/feature/discounts'
steps.expect: One new commit and a tiny diff.

steps.title: Round two: a fixup aimed at the right commit
steps.why: The second comment is about the second commit, not the tip. `--fixup` labels the response so it can be folded into the correct commit later, while still being an ordinary visible commit right now. Note which function it touches: a fixup whose diff overlaps lines added by a LATER commit conflicts when autosquash reorders it, so aim it at code the later commits leave alone.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit -q --fixup=$(git log --format=%H --grep="Apply discounts to order totals" -1)'

steps.expect: A commit literally titled 'fixup! Apply discounts to order totals'.

verify.contains: fixup! Apply discounts to order totals
verify.label: the second response is labelled against its target commit

steps.title: Approved — now tidy the series
steps.why: With review finished, autosquash folds each response into the commit it answered. The reviewer's ability to follow the conversation is no longer needed; the next reader's ability to follow the history is.
steps.expect: Three commits again, with no fixup markers, and every review response folded in.

verify.label: both review responses survived the squash

steps.title: Prove the tidy-up changed nothing but the history
steps.why: `range-diff` compares two versions of a branch commit by commit. Here it shows the same changes arranged differently — the check that makes a pre-merge cleanup safe to do without a second review.
steps.expect: An empty file diff: identical trees, cleaner series.

verify.label: the cleanup produced identical code
verify.hint: range-diff is how you prove a rewrite is honest

steps.title: Publish and merge
steps.why: The rewrite needs `--force-with-lease`, which is safe here because review is over and the branch is yours. Then an ordinary merge, and the branch is deleted.

verify.label: the tidied branch was merged and pushed
every review response is in the merged code
verify.hint: respond with commits, then autosquash before merging

verify.label: the server has the merge and the tidied series
the branch was cleaned up locally and on the server

pitfalls: Amending during review destroys the reviewer's place in the diff. Add commits while the conversation is live; squash only when it is over.
Force-pushing a branch under review is the most common complaint reviewers have. If you must, say so in a comment — the tooling cannot tell them.
`git range-diff <base> <old-tip> <new-tip>` is the tool that makes a pre-merge rewrite reviewable. Almost nobody knows it exists.
Keep a backup branch before an autosquash. It costs one command and turns a bad rebase into a one-line recovery.
If your forge squashes on merge anyway, the tidy-up matters less — but the commit messages it discards were the only record of what review changed.
cheatsheet: respond, labelled against an earlier commit
fold the responses in when review ends
